html:
Famadihana, the turning of the bones, is a funeral custom of the central highlands of Madagascar in which families open their ancestors' tombs, rewrap the bodies in fresh silk shrouds and dance with them.

It is held every few years in the dry season, with music, food and gatherings of the whole family. It honours the ancestors, who are believed to watch over the living, and many Christians practise it alongside church worship.

The custom grew among the Merina and Betsileo and is widely practised to this day, although some churches oppose it and an outbreak of plague in 2017 brought warnings about it. It shows how ancestor belief, kept at sites like Ambohimanga, shapes life in Madagascar.
sum: Famadihana, the turning of the bones, is a funeral custom of the central highlands of Madagascar in which families open their ancestors' tombs, rewrap the bodies in fresh silk shrouds and dance with them.
